EXTRA CLASS · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY

Every place in town, with its lesson on the card.

The town-map class: twenty-eight places walk the whole town in tour order — the places that teach us, the places that keep us safe, the food-and-shopping run, the quiet squares, the ways the town moves and the green places — and every tile below opens its own simple lesson a kid can follow.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Every place in town — with a lesson on its card.

The Places in the Community class is a bonus class, kept beside the main learning path like the Kitchen Helper and the Doctor Visit: the regular classes stay the core sequence, and this one is for the days when somebody asks what is that building? Twenty-eight places a town is made of — the library, the fire station, the bakery, the bus stop, the park — each one on its own card, and each card opens a simple lesson a kid can follow: what the place is, who works there, what we do there, step by step, and one way to play it at home tonight.

The places run in tour order on purpose. The learning places come first, because school is the building your child already owns; then the helping places, where doctors, dentists and the two stations keep everyone safe; then the food-and-shopping run; the quiet squares that make a town work; the ways the town moves; and the last group is the fresh air — gardens, parks, playgrounds, the zoo. By the end, the whole map of the town sits in one deck of cards.

THE PLACES, SIX WALKS OF TOWN

Twenty-eight cards, six kinds of places.

Twenty-eight places in six groups, in the order a real trip across town unfolds. Tap any picture and it opens its own simple lesson — the original card on the left, and the kid-followable guide on the right.

THE CLASS GAME

The Town Walk: build a street on the floor.

Stack the cards face down. Draw the top one, place it at the end of a growing "street" across the floor, and say what happens there — at the bakery, I buy bread! At the fire station, the truck sleeps! Card by card the street grows around the room until all twenty-eight places stand in a row, and then comes the best part: walk the whole town, end to end, and greet every stop on the way. Grown-ups walk it too — the losing shoe and the wrong turn are all part of the map.

SAME PLACE, TWO NAMES

Movie theater and cinema. Both are right.

Places travel even less than games do — the building never moves, but its name crosses the ocean and changes clothes. This class says so out loud. The cinema is the movie theater; the pharmacy is the drugstore or the chemist’s; the gas station sells petrol across the ocean; the dentist’s office is the dentist’s surgery in the UK; the sports center plays as the leisure centre; the shopping cart is a trolley; the garbage and trash are the rubbish; the street box is a mailbox or a post box; the pet shop is a pet store; and the airplane flies as the aeroplane. Whichever your family says, your child hears both — and learns early that places, like words, come in kinds.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

School — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what school is and what happens there, one step at a time.

What is this?

School is the place where children learn: letters, numbers, painting, songs, and how to be a good friend.

What does it mean?

Learning together is the big idea of school — a whole room of children discovering things on the same day, at the very same time.

What does the child need to know?

You need a coat hook with your name, a bag, and shoes that can run at playtime. The teachers do the rest.

Why this matters

School is where a town keeps its learning, and every grown-up you meet — bakers, doctors, drivers — went to a school just like yours first.

What it teaches

Following a routine, listening in a group, taking turns, and naming feelings on big days — school is a whole gym for growing up.

Words to learn

schoolteacherclassroomcoat hookcarpetstoryplaytimehome

Say this to your child

“"Good morning, school! I hang my coat, I find my spot on the carpet, and the day begins. Story time, snack time, playtime — and then home time!"”

Step by step

  1. Hang your coat on YOUR hook — the one with your name beside it.
  2. Find the carpet and sit cross-legged for morning hello.
  3. Learn something new: a letter, a number, a song.
  4. Play — blocks, paint, puzzles, friends.
  5. Snack, story, and then the best line of the day: someone at the door says "your grown-up is here!"

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the schoolhouse wears a clock on its roof and a flag on top, with a pink front door — the clock is the town’s promise that school starts on time, every single day.

Ask your child

"What is YOUR favorite thing at school?" "Who is the first person you say good morning to?" "What do we do when the clock says home time?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might march an entire column of toys to their own coat-hook lineup, sing the morning-hello song to the cat, or insist the pink door on the card is definitely the classroom door.

Out in the real world

Every town in the US, UK and Canada runs on its school — the building your child can already name is the same one their neighbors, cousins and future best friends walk into every morning.

Try it together

Play school at home: one child is the teacher, stuffed animals are the class, the carpet square is a cushion. Registration, story, snack — and home time comes exactly when the teacher says so.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the coat go?" (on YOUR hook) "What comes after learning time?" (playtime, then snack and story)

This lesson pairs with the School flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Library — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the library’s magic trick: take books home, bring them back, take more.

What is this?

A library is a place full of books that everyone may borrow — take some home, read them, and return them for the next reader.

What does it mean?

Sharing is the whole idea: one book on the shelf can be a hundred children’s favorite, one after another, for years.

What does the child need to know?

You need a library card (it looks very grown-up), a bag to carry the books home, and quiet feet for inside.

Why this matters

Every town keeps a library so that every child — any family, any day — can read as many books as they want, for free.

What it teaches

Book care, the borrowing loop (choose, keep safe, return), quiet-voice practice, and the proud feeling of a card with your name on it.

Words to learn

librarylibrarianborrowreturnshelfstory timelibrary cardquiet

Say this to your child

“"Shh — the library! We choose our books, the librarian goes beep, and the stories come home with us. We read them ALL, we keep them safe, and back they come for the next child!"”

Step by step

  1. Walk in with quiet feet — libraries listen.
  2. Explore the picture-book shelves: books live in rows like little houses.
  3. Pick your books — a good pile is about as tall as your arm.
  4. The librarian scans them — beep! — and the card does the magic.
  5. Read at home, keep them safe from juice, and bring every one back to borrow again.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, an open book is carved right above the library doors — the building shows everyone on the street exactly what lives inside.

Ask your child

"Who works here and helps us find books?" (the librarian) "What do we do with the books when we finish?" (bring them back) "What does the open book on the building mean?" (stories live here)

What your child can say or do

Your child might stamp everything in sight with a pretend library stamp, build a "bookshelf" out of couch cushions, or whisper for the rest of the day after a library visit — the quiet is contagious.

Out in the real world

Library cards are usually free from birth, story times run weekly in almost every US, UK and Canadian town, and many librarians will hunt down a book about dragons-on-trains just because a four-year-old asked.

Try it together

Play library at home: books lined on a shelf, a paper card for each family member, a stamp (or a sticker) for borrowing and returning. The librarian asks, "returns or new books today?"

Understanding check

Ask: "Do we buy the books?" (no — we borrow them) "And when we finish?" (we bring them back so the next child can read them)

This lesson pairs with the Library flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Museum — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what museums keep and how a small visitor walks one like a pro.

What is this?

A museum is a place that keeps old and wonderful things — dinosaur bones, paintings, rockets — so that everyone can come and see them.

What does it mean?

Keeping treasure together is the idea: a museum is a town’s memory with the lights left on.

What does the child need to know?

You need walking feet, looking eyes, and a quiet "wow" voice. Big museums have maps; small museums have smiles at the desk.

Why this matters

Some things are too old, too rare or too amazing to sit in anyone’s bedroom — the museum keeps them safe and shares them with every single person in town.

What it teaches

Careful looking (what IS that?), asking good questions, gentle behavior in shared spaces, and a first feel for long, long ago.

Words to learn

museumexhibittreasureoldbonespaintinglookguideticket

Say this to your child

“"Welcome to the museum! Old and wonderful things live here. We look with our eyes, we walk with quiet feet, and we say wow as many times as we like — wow is free!"”

Step by step

  1. Buy nothing — walk in, and the treasure is already yours to look at.
  2. Start with the loudest thing in the room (dinosaur, whale, rocket) — every museum has one.
  3. Look closely: what is it? how big? how old? Guess first, then read the sign with a grown-up.
  4. Walk — never run — between the treasures; the floors are proud of their quiet.
  5. Leave with a favorite: everyone names the best thing they saw, and it can be three different answers.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, tall stone columns hold up the museum front with a round emblem in the roof — museums dress like palaces so you know, before you even step in, that something grand is kept inside.

Ask your child

"What was your favorite treasure?" "Which was older — you or the dinosaur?" "What do our walking feet do in a museum?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might stand very still in front of the biggest exhibit and whisper "it’s REAL?", assign the dinosaur a name and a birthday, or open the visit with tickets they made themselves at home.

Out in the real world

Many museums have free days or free kids’ entry, and children’s museums in the US, UK and Canada are built for exactly this age — touch tables, dress-up corners, water rooms. The grand columns on the card are copied from ancient Greece.

Try it together

Home museum: three treasures on a table (a shiny stone, an old key, a feather), paper tickets, and a guide who tells one dramatic story about each exhibit. Guide rotates; admiring gasps required.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do our feet do in a museum?" (walk quietly) "Who keeps the treasures safe?" (the museum — and everyone who visits kindly)

This lesson pairs with the Museum flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

Cinema — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the whole trip to the movies — cinema to some families, movie theater to others — from ticket to credits.

What is this?

A cinema is a place with a giant screen and rows of seats, where everyone watches the same film at the same time in the dark.

What does it mean?

Watching together is the idea: a hundred strangers laugh at the same joke in the same second — that only happens in a cinema.

What does the child need to know?

You need a ticket (one per person, even tiny ones), a seat number, and popcorn — sharing the bucket is traditional.

Why this matters

Films are made enormous on purpose: the screen is taller than the house so that dragons feel real and oceans look endless.

What it teaches

Sitting with a group, watching a story the whole way through, quiet-voice whispers, and the big feeling of lights-down excitement.

Words to learn

cinemamoviescreenticketseatpopcornlightsfilmcredits

Say this to your child

“"One ticket, please! Popcorn — thank you! Find seat number 5... lights going down... hush... the film is starting! Shhh — watch — did you SEE that?!"”

Step by step

  1. Choose the film at the window or the board — today is decided by YOU.
  2. Hand over the ticket; the ticket person tears it in half — that is the good part.
  3. Popcorn first: the smell is the overture.
  4. Find your seat by the number, sit down, and hush — the lights dim, the screen wakes.
  5. Watch to the very end — the lights come up, and that is when the clapping happens.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, little lights ring the cinema front and a film-reel sign spins over the double doors — the marquee is the cinema shouting its film to the whole street.

Ask your child

"Who tears the ticket?" "What happens when the lights go down?" (the film starts — and we hush) "What do we say when the film is wonderful?" (clap! cheer! again!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might tear every paper ticket with enormous ceremony, narrate the popcorn like a sports announcer, or whisper "shh, it’s starting" to the entire sofa before home films.

Out in the real world

American families say movie theater; British and Canadian families say cinema — same seats, same popcorn, same trailers. A first film trip goes best with a short film and an early showing; home practice counts.

Try it together

Home cinema night: dim the lamps, line up the chairs, tear paper tickets, popcorn in cups, and a "trailer" — someone announces tomorrow’s story in a big voice. Lights down. Film on.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do when the lights go down?" (hush and watch) "Where does the popcorn go?" (in the bucket — and then in us)

This lesson pairs with the Cinema flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hospital — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what a hospital is and who works inside, so the big building feels like the helper it is.

What is this?

A hospital is a big place where doctors and nurses help people get better — broken arms, fevers, check-ups, and brand-new babies.

What does it mean?

Everyone helping everyone is the idea: a hospital is the town’s biggest promise that nobody is left hurt.

What does the child need to know?

You need to know your name and your grown-up’s name — hospitals ask both kindly. Wristbands go on, stickers come off (onto you).

Why this matters

Some hurts are too big for home — the hospital keeps everything a body could need in one building, with people who practice helping every single day.

What it teaches

Naming body feelings (hurts, hot, dizzy), trusting helpers, sitting through a wait, and the brave skill of letting a stranger with a kind voice look in your ears.

Words to learn

hospitaldoctornursepatientbandagestethoscopewristbandbetter

Say this to your child

“"This is the hospital, where the helpers work. The doctor looks in my ears — bloop! — listens to my heart — thump, thump — and says, all better soon! Sticker, please!"”

Step by step

  1. Walk in together — hands held, name known.
  2. Tell the desk who you are: "I am here with my grown-up."
  3. Wait your turn — hospitals run on turns; the toys are there for the waiting.
  4. Let the doctor look: ears, throat, tummy — say ahh and let the cold disc do its job.
  5. Collect the sticker (non-negotiable), wave goodbye to the nurses, and go home feeling proud.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a big cross sits on the hospital front above rows of windows — almost the whole world agrees that this sign means "people who help are inside".

Ask your child

"Who helps people at the hospital?" (doctors and nurses) "What does the cross on the building mean?" (helpers inside) "What do we tell the desk?" (our name and our grown-up’s name)

What your child can say or do

Your child might bandage every teddy limb in the house, listen to everyone’s heart with a cardboard tube and a very serious face, or hand out stickers after each "check-up" like a tiny discharge nurse.

Out in the real world

Many hospitals run teddy-bear clinics where the toy gets the tour, and knowing the rooms before a real visit changes everything — a familiar hospital is half as scary as a first one. New babies are born here too: hospitals are where towns grow.

Try it together

Hospital for toys: one teddy with a sore paw, one dolly with a cough. Bandage with toilet paper, listen with the tube, write a prescription (a drawing), and finish with a sticker — hospitals always have stickers.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who works at the hospital?" (doctors and nurses) "And what do they do all day?" (help people get better)

This lesson pairs with the Hospital flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Dentist’s Office — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the whole tooth check-up, step by step, so the chair feels like a game before the real visit.

What is this?

A dentist’s office is where teeth get their check-ups: counted, cleaned, and protected from sugar bugs.

What does it mean?

Small habits, big teeth: the dentist is the coach who helps your smile win every day.

What does the child need to know?

You need brave sitting, an open mouth on request, and a toothbrush working at home twice a day — the dentist sees everything, you know.

Why this matters

Teeth are the only bones we show the world — and the only ones that can get holes. The dentist finds tiny trouble while it is still tiny.

What it teaches

Opening wide on request, sitting in a chair that leans, naming teeth (front, pointy, big grinders), and the twice-a-day brushing habit.

Words to learn

dentistteethtoothcheck-upmirrorpolishsugar bugsstickeropen wide

Say this to your child

“"Hop in the chair, open wide — AHH! The dentist counts: one, two, three... all here! No sugar bugs today! Now the polish — bzzzz — tickle, tickle — all shiny! Sticker, please!"”

Step by step

  1. Climb into the big chair — it leans back like a rocket ready for launch.
  2. Open wide and say ahh — the little mirror hops in for a look around.
  3. Count the teeth out loud: how many live in there today?
  4. Hunt for sugar bugs — spot them before they build a house.
  5. Polish! The spinning brush tickles, the teeth shine, and the treasure box pays out the sticker.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a giant tooth hangs over the striped awning of the dentist’s office — nobody ever has to guess who works in this building.

Ask your child

"What do we say to open wide?" (ahh!) "Who counts our teeth?" (the dentist) "How do we keep sugar bugs away at home?" (brush, brush, brush — twice a day)

What your child can say or do

Your child might count the family’s teeth at dinner (up to 32 per grown-up, they will learn), play dentist with a spoon mirror and a very firm "open wider, please", or demand the polish sound "bzzz" during bedtime brushing.

Out in the real world

American families visit the dentist’s office; British families visit the dentist’s surgery — same chair, same mirror, same sticker. First visits are kept short and friendly on purpose: sit, count, polish, treasure box, done.

Try it together

Doll dentist: count all the doll’s teeth out loud, check with a spoon for a mirror, brush every single one with a real toothbrush, and pay for the visit with one pretend coin. The counting IS the practice.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we say for the dentist?" (open wide — ahh!) "How do we beat the sugar bugs?" (brushing twice a day, and the dentist’s polish)

This lesson pairs with the Dentist’s Office flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Pharmacy — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches how medicine travels from doctor to pharmacy to home — and the one rule that rides along.

What is this?

A pharmacy is a shop where medicine is kept and given out by a pharmacist, exactly the amount the doctor ordered.

What does it mean?

Right medicine, right person, right amount: the pharmacist is the town’s medicine referee.

What does the child need to know?

You need the doctor’s paper (the prescription), a grown-up’s hand to carry it in, and patience — good medicine is counted, not rushed.

Why this matters

Medicine is powerful — that is the whole point — so it lives behind the counter with a person who knows exactly how much is right for you.

What it teaches

Understanding "medicine is not candy", waiting at a counter, naming helpers (doctor writes, pharmacist fills, grown-up gives), and the safety habit for life.

Words to learn

pharmacydrugstorechemistpharmacistprescriptionmedicinecounterdose

Say this to your child

“"Here is the doctor’s paper! The pharmacist reads it, counts the medicine — one, two, three — and writes my name on the bottle. Medicine rides home with a grown-up. That is the rule, and it keeps me safe!"”

Step by step

  1. The doctor writes a paper — the prescription — just for you.
  2. A grown-up hands the paper over the pharmacy counter.
  3. The pharmacist counts and pours: exactly the right amount, no more.
  4. The label gets your name on it — read it together: that says YOU.
  5. The bag goes home with the grown-up, and the grown-up gives the medicine — that is the one rule, said kindly, every time.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the cross shines above the pharmacy windows — in many towns this is the shop whose lights stay on latest, because helpers close last.

Ask your child

"Who fills the prescription?" (the pharmacist) "Whose name goes on the label?" (yours) "Who gives the medicine at home?" (a grown-up — always)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sort pom-pom "medicine" into bottles with hospital-grade seriousness, stamp every doll label with their own name, or recite the safety rule to the cat unprompted — repeat customers are the goal.

Out in the real world

American families say drugstore; British families say chemist’s or pharmacy — the counter works the same everywhere. Pharmacists answer questions for free, and many will show a child the counting tray if asked at a quiet moment.

Try it together

Pharmacy at home: colored pom-poms in pill bottles, sorted by color and size, labels drawn on with names. One rule repeated kindly while playing — medicine is only for grown-ups to give.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who counts the medicine?" (the pharmacist) "And who gives it to you at home?" (a grown-up — never yourself, never from the bottle)

This lesson pairs with the Pharmacy flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Fire Station — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches who waits inside the fire station and what happens the second the bell rings.

What is this?

A fire station is where firefighters eat, sleep, exercise and wait — with the fire truck parked inside, ready to roll out in one minute.

What does it mean?

Ready is the whole idea: firefighters do not know when the bell will ring, so they practice being ready every minute of every day.

What does the child need to know?

You need to hear the famous facts: the pole (for fast), the boots (beside the bed, pointing out), the dalmatian (tradition), and the minute (all they allow themselves).

Why this matters

Fires and emergencies cannot wait — so the station keeps everything a rescue needs under one roof, parked, fueled, and pointed at the door.

What it teaches

Understanding "ready" as a skill, emergency vocabulary (bell, siren, rescue), respect for sirens on the street, and the fun of gear-up speed games.

Words to learn

fire stationfirefighterfire truckfire enginepolebootsbellsirenrescue

Say this to your child

“"This is the fire station! The truck is sleeping — shh — and the boots are waiting by the bed. Bell rings! DING-DING-DING! Down the pole, on with the boots, WHOOSH — off to help!"”

Step by step

  1. Look at the big doors — they open like a garage because the truck is a very tall, very fast member of the family.
  2. Find the pole: when the bell rings, firefighters slide down instead of taking the stairs. Seconds matter.
  3. The boots sleep beside the beds, pointing at the truck — jump in, feet first, done.
  4. The bell rings: pole, boots, helmet, truck — WHOOSH out of the doors, siren singing.
  5. Rescue done, truck home, washed and parked and ready again — that is the whole day, and it repeats.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the red fire truck waits between two big garage doors under the flame badge — the doors are tall because the truck must leave in a hurry and come home the same way.

Ask your child

"Where do the boots sleep?" (beside the bed, pointing out) "What do firefighters do when the bell rings?" (pole, boots, truck — go!) "What is the truck’s color?" (red — always red)

What your child can say or do

Your child might slide down the sofa arm "down the pole", gear up in rain boots at astonishing speed when anyone rings a bell, or assign the dalmatian a firehouse job title of their own invention.

Out in the real world

American families say fire truck; British families say fire engine — same red, same siren. Fire stations welcome visits in all three countries, and many hand out plastic helmets; ask at a quiet time, not mid-emergency.

Try it together

Bell rings, boots on: someone rings an imaginary bell, and the firefighter must put on shoes, hat and "air tank" backpack and run to the door — timed, cheered, repeated. Ready-in-a-hurry is the game AND the real skill.

Understanding check

Ask: "What happens when the bell rings?" (slide the pole, boots on, truck out) "How long do firefighters give themselves?" (about a minute — ready!)

This lesson pairs with the Fire Station flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Police Station — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches who works at the police station and how an officer helps — including the friendly version of the lost-child plan.

What is this?

A police station is where police officers work: they start their rounds here, keep lost things safe here, and help anyone who knocks, any hour.

What does it mean?

Keeping everyone safe is the idea — the badge means "you can ask me for help", and the station is where that promise lives.

What does the child need to know?

You need to know your own name and a grown-up’s name — the two most powerful words in any lost moment. Officers know the rest.

Why this matters

Every town needs helpers who never sleep: while the town dreams, someone answers the phone, checks the streets, and walks the lost bicycle home.

What it teaches

Safety vocabulary (lost, helper, badge), the name-and-grown-up drill, trust in uniforms, and kind understanding of "people who work while we sleep".

Words to learn

policeofficerbadgestationsafelostfoundhelpuniform

Say this to your child

“"This is the police station — helpers work here, day and night. The badge means: you can ask me! If I am ever lost, I find an officer and say my name and my grown-up’s name — and the helping begins."”

Step by step

  1. See the badge — a star on a shield — the same star officers wear on their chest and their patrol car.
  2. Officers start the day here: roll call, radio check, and off into the town.
  3. Lost things come here: bicycles, gloves, teddy bears — the shelf waits patiently.
  4. If a child is lost, the plan is simple and strong: find a police officer (or a parent with children), say your name and your grown-up’s name, and stay together until found.
  5. The station never closes — somebody is there right now, tonight, and every night.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a star sits on a shield-shaped badge over the police station doors — the same design the officers carry, so a child can match the building to the helper.

Ask your child

"Who works at the police station?" (police officers) "What does the badge mean?" (you can ask me for help) "What do we say if we are lost?" (our name and our grown-up’s name)

What your child can say or do

Your child might badge every drawing with a star and shield, radio the dinner table ("officer requesting snacks"), or practice the lost-plan on every walk — pointing out officers and whispering "helpers".

Out in the real world

In the US, UK and Canada the lost-child plan is the same: find a police officer or a parent with children and say your name. Practicing it as a game turns the scariest moment into a known routine — that is this card’s whole job.

Try it together

The friendly-officer game: one toy walks a cushion street and gets "lost"; the officer asks kindly questions — name, who we are looking for — and walks everyone home. Reunion hug required by law.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who can we ask for help if we are lost?" (a police officer) "What do we tell them?" (our name and our grown-up’s name)

This lesson pairs with the Police Station flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Supermarket — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the whole supermarket trip, from grabbing the cart to the beeping at the till.

What is this?

A supermarket is one big store with all the food in it — fruit, bread, milk, cheese, cereal — lined up in long aisles.

What does it mean?

Gathering is the idea: the whole town’s kitchens come shopping in one roof, aisle by aisle.

What does the child need to know?

You need a cart (or a trolley), a list (pictures count!), and your walking feet — the aisles are long and the wheels are tempting.

Why this matters

No family could grow or make everything it eats — the supermarket collects it all so one trip fills a whole week.

What it teaches

List-following, matching picture to shelf, gentle aisle manners (walk, don’t wheel), and the checkout sequence — unload, beep, pay, carry.

Words to learn

supermarketstoreshopcarttrolleyaislelisttillcheckoutbag

Say this to your child

“"Cart — check! List — check! Aisle one: apples — found them! Cross it off. The cold aisle — brrr! Milk and cheese. Now the till goes beep, beep, beep — all paid — and I carry the bag. Shopping done!"”

Step by step

  1. Grab a cart — click the wheels, take the driver’s seat (for a passenger, that is).
  2. Read the first thing on the list: apples! Now hunt the aisles — apples live with the fruit.
  3. Weigh or count, drop gently in the cart, and cross it off — NEXT!
  4. The cold aisle is an expedition: milk, cheese, yogurt — doors that open into winter.
  5. The till: unload, beep beep beep, pay, and the proud job — carrying the first bag to the car.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the shopping-cart sign rolls over the supermarket entrance under wide front windows — the sign tells every hungry passerby exactly what happens inside.

Ask your child

"What do we push around the store?" (a cart — or a trolley in the UK) "What is on YOUR list?" "What does the till say when the food goes over it?" (beep, beep, beep)

What your child can say or do

Your child might march the aisles with the list held like a treasure map, interrogate every shelf ("but WHERE do the eggs live?"), or take the bag-carrying job so seriously the bag outlives the shopping.

Out in the real world

American and Canadian families push a shopping cart; British families push a trolley — and the store is a shop on one shore and a store on the other. The picture list is the universal move: every family does it, and it works in all three countries.

Try it together

Home supermarket: cans and boxes lined on a shelf, a basket, a paper list of five foods, and a till that beeps (a spoon on a box works). Shopper shops, cashier beeps, and then the roles swap.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we bring with us?" (a cart and a list) "What happens at the till?" (beep — pay — carry)

This lesson pairs with the Supermarket flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bakery — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the best-smelling errand in town — ordering at the bakery, one bun at a time.

What is this?

A bakery is a shop where bread and buns are baked fresh every morning by a baker who starts before the sun.

What does it mean?

Everyday magic is the idea: flour, water and a hot oven turn into breakfast, in a building everyone can smell from the corner.

What does the child need to know?

You need your order ready ("one bun, please!"), a paper bag to carry it in, and hands that can resist until the front door.

Why this matters

Bread is the oldest store-bought food in the world, and every town keeps a place where it is made the old way — by hand, in the dark, hours before anyone wakes.

What it teaches

Ordering out loud, counting the order, waiting while it is wrapped, and the manners that get a "thank you, see you tomorrow!" from the baker.

Words to learn

bakerybakerbreadbunloafovenorderbagfresh

Say this to your child

“"Smell that? The bakery! Good morning, baker! Three buns, please — one, two, three in the bag. Thank you! The bag is warm... I am holding breakfast!"”

Step by step

  1. Follow your nose down the street — the bakery advertises by smell alone.
  2. Look in the case: buns, loaves, croissants, the jam ones in the back.
  3. Order out loud and by count: "Three buns, please!" — the baker hears you the first time.
  4. The bag goes warm in your hands — that is the bread telling you it is fresh.
  5. Say thank you, and if a corner of the loaf disappears before home — the baker understands. It is tradition.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the striped awning shades the bakery window and the shelves stand full of golden rolls — the shop shows its bread right in the window, because fresh bread needs no poster.

Ask your child

"Who bakes the bread?" (the baker — starting very early) "What do we say to order?" (one bun, please — or three!) "How do we know the bread is fresh?" (the bag is warm)

What your child can say or do

Your child might line up play-dough buns by size, take orders from every stuffed animal with a notepad, or narrate the walk home from a real bakery like a heist movie: "nobody touch the bag."

Out in the real world

A bakery sells bread, a bakeshop leans toward cakes, and the corner shop in the UK, US and Canada usually covers both. Watching the morning bread delivery — the racks, the tongs, the steam — is a free street show in every town.

Try it together

Bakery shop at home: play-dough rolls, a paper apron, a tray, and customers who order by count — "three buns, please!" Counting out the order is the math; the paper bag is the theater.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who bakes the bread and when?" (the baker — before the sun) "What do our hands feel when the bread is fresh?" (a warm bag)

This lesson pairs with the Bakery flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Farmers’ Market — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches how a farmers’ market works — the food travels ten steps from the farm table to your bag.

What is this?

A farmers’ market is an open-air market where farmers sell what they grew — carrots, corn, berries — stall by stall, often in the town square.

What does it mean?

Meeting your food is the idea: at the market, the person behind the tomatoes is the person who watered them.

What does the child need to know?

You need a bag or basket, small coins, and a question ready — farmers love questions about their crops and will usually answer with a sample.

Why this matters

Market food was in the ground this week — that is why the carrots still have their tops and the corn is sweeter than any store’s.

What it teaches

Season naming (strawberries in June, squash in October), sampling manners, buying with real coins, and naming colors, shapes and plants on sight.

Words to learn

farmmarketfarmerstallcropscarrotscornberriessampleseason

Say this to your child

“"The farmers’ market! Did YOU grow these carrots? — wow! Can I try one? Crunch! Sweet! I’ll take five, please. Thank you, farmer! See you next market day!"”

Step by step

  1. Walk in and look at EVERYTHING first — the market is one long rainbow.
  2. Find the grower: "Did you grow these carrots?" The answer is always yes, with pride.
  3. Try the sample — one bite, honest chewing, verdict delivered ("sweet!").
  4. Choose and count your crops; the farmer bags them and takes the coins.
  5. Carry the bag like a champion and name every crop on the walk home — three colors of green counts as three.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the stall’s striped awning shades crates of carrots and leafy greens piled high — market food arrives in crates, not boxes, and the green tops are its passport.

Ask your child

"Who grew the corn at the market?" (the farmer — and they are standing right there) "What do we say after a sample?" (thank you — and our honest verdict!) "Which foods come in autumn?" (apples, squash, pumpkins...)

What your child can say or do

Your child might interview every farmer ("how heavy is a pumpkin?"), pay with coins counted one by one, or establish a market-day tradition so fixed that the carrot farmer knows their order by heart.

Out in the real world

Markets run on the season’s calendar in the US, UK and Canada — asparagus in May, strawberries in June, pumpkins in October — so the same stall teaches the whole year. Many markets have music and kids’ stalls; go early, go hungry.

Try it together

Market morning at home: fruits and vegetables on a blanket, one farmer and one shopper, play coins, and a rule — the farmer must name every crop and answer one question about it ("how DO carrots grow?").

Understanding check

Ask: "Who sells the food at the farmers’ market?" (the farmers who grew it) "Why do the carrots have green tops?" (they were in the ground this week)

This lesson pairs with the Farmers’ Market flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Restaurant — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the grand theater of eating out — ordering, waiting, and the miracle of no dishes.

What is this?

A restaurant is a place where a kitchen cooks your order and a waiter brings it to your table — you choose, they cook, nobody at your table washes up.

What does it mean?

Taking turns serving each other is the idea: tonight the restaurant serves you, and learning to be served kindly is a skill of its own.

What does the child need to know?

You need your inside voice, your order decided (decide BEFORE the waiter arrives), and both magic words loaded: please and thank you.

Why this matters

Restaurants let a family celebrate ordinary Tuesdays — and they run on manners so smooth that nobody notices them, which is exactly what practicing them at a young age builds.

What it teaches

Ordering for yourself, patience between ordering and arriving, table manners, and thanking the waiter — the full social meal, rehearsed.

Words to learn

restaurantmenuwaiterorderkitchentabledessertbillthank you

Say this to your child

“"Welcome! Table for three, please! I read the menu... I order: pasta, please! The kitchen clatters, the waiter brings the plates — hot hot hot! Thank you! And the best part: no dishes for us tonight!"”

Step by step

  1. Sit down and unfold the menu — pictures are legal, ordering by picture is a classic move.
  2. Decide. Once the waiter stands there, the window for "ummm" is short.
  3. Order with the magic words: "Pasta, please!" — the waiter writes it down, which makes it official.
  4. Wait together — conversations, crayons, bread basket. Good things are cooking.
  5. Feast, say thank you to the waiter, and leave the plates — THAT is the restaurant’s whole trick.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the fork-and-plate sign hangs over the restaurant awning — the whole world reads this sign the same way: sit down, someone will come.

Ask your child

"What do we read at a restaurant?" (the menu) "How do we order?" ("pasta, please!") "Who washes the dishes?" (the restaurant — not us!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might run the whole notepad-and-towel-arm waiter routine for dinner, "take orders" from every relative on the phone, or order dessert with such gravity that the waiter brings two spoons.

Out in the real world

In the UK a small casual restaurant is often called a caff or a bistro; in the US and Canada, a diner — every town has its own flavor. Children who order for themselves at restaurants learn a portable skill: asking strangers, politely, for what they want.

Try it together

Paper-menu restaurant tonight: draw tonight’s real dinner as a menu with pictures, take the family’s order with a notepad, serve with a towel over the arm, and present the "bill" for payment in hugs.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do before the waiter comes?" (decide our order) "And the two magic words tonight?" (please and thank you)

This lesson pairs with the Restaurant flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Pet Shop — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches how to visit a pet shop like a kind person — and what every pet actually needs.

What is this?

A pet shop is a store full of animals and their supplies: fish in tanks, a dog in the window, a cat on a cushion, and shelves of food and toys.

What does it mean?

Pets are promises, not toys: every animal in the window needs food, a home and a kind family for its whole life.

What does the child need to know?

You need quiet voices (animals startle), gentle fingers (only where the shop says), and the honesty to know that looking is today’s job.

Why this matters

The pet shop is where families and animals meet — doing it kindly, and knowing what a pet needs BEFORE taking one home, is how good pets and good children happen.

What it teaches

Gentle-touch practice, empathy (what does the puppy need?), responsibility talk (feeding, walking, cleaning), and the difference between wanting and promising.

Words to learn

petpet shoppet storedogcatfishhamsterfoodadoptgentle

Say this to your child

“"The pet shop! Hello, dog in the window — hello, cat! Quiet voices... gentle fingers... Every animal here needs food, a bed and a kind family. Today we look. One day — a big promise!"”

Step by step

  1. Visit the window first — the dog and cat are the greeters, and they are working.
  2. Watch quietly: what is the puppy doing? What is the cat pretending not to do?
  3. Tour the tanks: fish, and the hamster on its wheel (a hamster runs up to five miles a night — on a wheel the size of a plate).
  4. Learn the shopping list: every animal needs food, a bed, water, and a vet — say it like a spell.
  5. Looking is free; adopting is a big promise. The pet shop teaches both, in one visit.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the paw-print sign hangs over the pet shop window where a dog and a cat look out at the street — the shop’s two official greeters, on duty every day.

Ask your child

"What does every pet need?" (food, water, a bed and a kind family) "What kind of voices do we use at the pet shop?" (quiet ones) "Is looking free?" (yes — adopting is the big promise)

What your child can say or do

Your child might name every animal in the window (twice, in case they forgot), run a stuffed-animal adoption agency with paperwork, or announce at dinner that the family’s future dog has already been chosen — by them, just now.

Out in the real world

American families say pet store; British families say pet shop — same window, same puppies. The visit is also the gentlest rehearsal for the real adoption talk: a pet is not a toy, it is a small promise kept every single day.

Try it together

Adoption day: every stuffed animal in the house lines up, the shop opens, and the customer picks one to "adopt" — with a promise to feed it, brush it and love it forever, signed with a crayon X.

Understanding check

Ask: "Is a pet a toy?" (no — a promise) "What do we use in the pet shop?" (quiet voices and gentle fingers)

This lesson pairs with the Pet Shop flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bank — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what a bank does — money in, money out, kept safe the whole time.

What is this?

A bank is a building where grown-ups keep their money safe, take some out when they need it, and save some for later.

What does it mean?

Safekeeping is the idea: the bank is the town’s treasure room, and the big vault door inside is thicker than the front door of a castle.

What does the child need to know?

You need to know the two machines: the counter inside (for people) and the ATM outside — the cashpoint — that works day and night.

Why this matters

Keeping money under the mattress is risky and hard to count — the bank counts it perfectly, keeps it safe, and even lets savings grow a little.

What it teaches

First money vocabulary (save, spend, deposit), counting coins, and the big idea that machines can be trusted helpers when they are built for the job.

Words to learn

bankmoneysavespendvaultATMcashpointcoinsdeposit

Say this to your child

“"This is the bank — the town’s treasure room! Money goes IN to be safe, money comes OUT when we need it. And look, the money machine! Card in, code in — clunk, clunk — coins for ice cream day!"”

Step by step

  1. Look up at the columns — banks are built strong on purpose, so everyone trusts them.
  2. Inside, a teller sits behind glass and helps: money IN (a deposit) or money OUT (a withdrawal).
  3. Outside stands the money machine — the ATM, or cashpoint — with a screen, buttons, and a slot that whispers to cards.
  4. The card goes in, the secret code goes in, and the machine counts out exactly what was asked for.
  5. Money back in the pocket, receipt in hand — the town’s treasure is always exactly where it should be.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, stone columns stand guard and a round coin sits in the bank’s roof — banks have looked grand and strong for thousands of years so that everyone knows: what is mine is safe in here.

Ask your child

"What do grown-ups keep at the bank?" (money — safe) "What is the money machine called?" (the ATM — or the cashpoint in the UK) "What do we do with money we want to keep?" (save it)

What your child can say or do

Your child might run a cereal-box teller window at the kitchen table, count the piggy bank into "deposits" and "withdrawals", or demand to press the buttons at the real cashpoint with the gravity of a vault inspector.

Out in the real world

American families use the ATM; British families say cashpoint or hole-in-the-wall — same machine, same beeping. The card is a first money lesson in disguise: money goes in, money comes out, and saving is the game that wins.

Try it together

Family bank: a cereal box with a teller window, buttons as deposits, receipts scribbled on paper. The teller counts every deposit twice, and savings that reach ten coins earn a family dance.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the bank do with money?" (keeps it safe) "What do we call the outside machine in the UK?" (the cashpoint)

This lesson pairs with the Bank flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Post Office — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches how a letter travels — from your hand, through the post office, all the way to a door far away.

What is this?

A post office is where letters and parcels begin their journeys: weighed, stamped, and sent off to addresses everywhere.

What does it mean?

Connection is the idea: the post office is how the town holds hands with the whole world, one envelope at a time.

What does the child need to know?

You need the address written clearly, a stamp in the corner, and a box or envelope that closes — the mail carrier does the rest.

Why this matters

Emails are instant, but a LETTER is paper you can hold, drawn on, and keep in a box forever — and something has to carry it: trucks, trains, planes, and one person on your street.

What it teaches

Address writing (name, street, town), understanding a journey in steps, weighing (light and heavy), and the patience of mail — it arrives when it arrives.

Words to learn

post officemailpostletterparcelstampscalemail carrierpostieaddress

Say this to your child

“"Dear Grandma... done! Stamp on — press! At the post office: ploop, on the scale — not too heavy! Now it rides the van, the train, the plane... and in three days: MAIL for Grandma! I sent that!"”

Step by step

  1. Write or draw the letter — and put the person’s name and address on the front, clear as a lighthouse.
  2. Fold it into the envelope and press the stamp on the corner — the stamp is the ticket that pays for the journey.
  3. At the post office, the parcel hops on the scale — ploop — light ones cost less, heavy ones cost more.
  4. Off it goes: van, sorting room, truck, train, plane — wherever the address says.
  5. A mail carrier (a postie!) walks it to the door, and somebody shouts "MAIL!" — the best word on any street.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a big envelope rides above the post office doors — the only sign in town that promises somebody a journey.

Ask your child

"What pays for the letter’s trip?" (the stamp) "Who brings the mail to our door?" (the mail carrier — the postie) "What goes on the envelope so it finds the right house?" (the name and address)

What your child can say or do

Your child might sticker-stamp every envelope in the house, weigh toys on the bathroom scale "just like the post office", or wait by the window at mail time like a lighthouse keeper watching for ships.

Out in the real world

The building is the post office everywhere, but the street box is a mailbox in the US and Canada and a post box in the UK, and the person is a mail carrier or a postie. Four words, one journey — and the stamp goes top-right in all three countries.

Try it together

The full mail loop at home: write a real letter to someone in the house, stamp it with stickers, deliver it through a door-slot or under a pillow, and wait for the reply. Sending AND receiving — both halves are magic.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where does the stamp go?" (the corner — top right) "Who walks the letter to the door?" (the mail carrier / postie)

This lesson pairs with the Post Office flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hair Salon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the whole haircut visit, from the tall chair to the big mirror moment.

What is this?

A hair salon is where hair is washed, cut and combed by a stylist — every visit ends with a fresh new look in the mirror.

What does it mean?

Confidence is the idea: a haircut is small change that makes a person stand taller — the salon sells the sparkle, not just the trim.

What does the child need to know?

You need a still head (the most important tool), a yes to the cape, and something to look at in the mirror — many salons keep a stool of books exactly for this.

Why this matters

Hair keeps growing and growing — someone has to keep it tidy, and the salon does it with warm water, snippy scissors and a great final reveal.

What it teaches

Sitting still for a stretch, trusting a helper with sharp tools (kept kindly away from little fingers), naming the tools, and enjoying a healthy new routine.

Words to learn

salonstylisthairdresserbarberscissorscombcapewashmirrortrim

Say this to your child

“"Welcome to the hair salon! Up we go — the chair rises! Cape on — whoosh! Wash, wash, bubbly bubbles... comb and snip, snip, snip... and SPIN — the mirror shows the brand-new me! Hello, new me!"”

Step by step

  1. Climb into the big chair — it goes UP with a lever, like a throne.
  2. The cape flies over you — whoosh — now you are a haircut astronaut.
  3. The wash: warm water, bubbly shampoo, a head massage that makes everyone go quiet.
  4. The cut: comb, snip, comb, snip — hair falls like confetti and YOU sit wonderfully still.
  5. The reveal: the chair spins to the mirror — look! The new you waves back. Tip optional, wave mandatory.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, a scissors-and-comb sign hangs over the salon door with swirly curls painted on the windows — the swirls are the hair, the scissors are the promise.

Ask your child

"What flies over you before the haircut?" (the cape) "What do we do with our head while the stylist cuts?" (hold it still — like a statue) "What does the mirror show at the end?" (the brand-new you)

What your child can say or do

Your child might spin every doll to "the mirror part", drape towel capes on the whole family, or hold their head statue-still with such pride that the stylist compliments the sitting like an Olympic sport.

Out in the real world

American families go to the salon or the barber; British families go to the hairdresser’s — same chair, same cape, same mirror. First haircuts famously come with certificates and a lock of hair in an envelope; the chair is the milestone.

Try it together

Salon day for the dolls: towel capes all around, a spray-bottle wash, a pretend trim with finger-scissors, and the big mirror reveal with a gasp of admiration — "and NOW... the big finish!"

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do while the stylist cuts?" (hold still) "What does the cape do?" (flies over you — whoosh)

This lesson pairs with the Hair Salon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Hotel — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what hotels are for and how a stay works — from the front desk to the checkout time.

What is this?

A hotel is a building full of bedrooms that travelers rent for a night or a few — with a desk that hands out keys and sometimes breakfast downstairs.

What does it mean?

A home away from home is the idea: the hotel keeps a bed ready for people who are far from theirs.

What does the child need to know?

You need a suitcase, a key card (it beeps), and the knowledge that room numbers are like addresses in a tall building — 204 is on floor 2.

Why this matters

Families travel — to visit cousins, to see the ocean, to explore a city — and every traveler needs a safe bed; hotels keep thousands of them ready at once.

What it teaches

Sequencing a stay (check in, sleep, check out), number recognition for room doors, the independence of a "my own room" night, and travel manners with strangers who are all being kind.

Words to learn

hoteltravelercheck incheck outkey cardroom numberlobbysuitcasevacationholiday

Say this to your child

“"The hotel! One room for my family, please! Key card — beep! Floor two, door two-oh-four — beep — the door opens! A bed, a window, tiny shampoos! Tonight I sleep in a hotel, far from home, like a traveler!"”

Step by step

  1. Walk into the lobby with the suitcase — wheels singing on the floor.
  2. Check in at the front desk: "We have a reservation!" The desk hands over the key card.
  3. Find the room by number — floor 2, door 204 — beep, and the door opens. EVERY time, the beep is exciting.
  4. Explore the room: the bed (bigger than yours?), the window (whose town is THAT?), the tiny shampoos (keepable, the small ones).
  5. Sleep like a traveler, pack like a pro, and check out by the time on the door sign — "thank you, bye-bye, hotel!"

Look closer at the picture

On the card, three stars shine over the hotel’s rows of windows — every window is somebody’s room for the night, and the stars promise a good one.

Ask your child

"Who hands out the key cards?" (the desk at check-in) "What does the key card do?" (beeps the door open) "What do we do in the morning?" (pack, and check out — bye-bye, hotel)

What your child can say or do

Your child might pack a suitcase for a one-night living-room trip, beep every door in the house with an invisible card, or guard the tiny shampoo bottles with customs-officer energy.

Out in the real world

British families go on holiday; American and Canadian families go on vacation — and both sleep in hotels. The card teaches the whole portable routine — check in, sleep, check out, thank you — which works the same in every country’s lobby.

Try it together

Home hotel: a suitcase packed for one night in the living room, paper keys handed over the "front desk", room service (crackers and juice) ordered by telephone, checkout by 11 — as the sign says.

Understanding check

Ask: "What happens first — check in or check out?" (check in) "What sound does the key card make?" (beep!)

This lesson pairs with the Hotel flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Gas Station — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what happens when the car gets hungry — the whole gas station visit, from pull-in to snack.

What is this?

A gas station is where cars drink their fuel: pumps under a big canopy, a little shop, and sometimes air for tires and a wash for windows.

What does it mean?

Cars work on fuel the way kids work on food — the gas station is the town’s kitchen for cars, open late and always pouring.

What does the child need to know?

You need to know the golden rule: the pumps are a grown-up zone — small hands watch from the car seat, and that is the whole job, and it is an important one.

Why this matters

No fuel, no go — every car in town visits a gas station every week or so, which makes it one of the busiest doorsteps in the neighborhood.

What it teaches

Patience in the car seat, count-along filling (count to ten with the pump), naming the car’s needs (fuel, clean windshield, tires), and the safety habit: look, don’t touch.

Words to learn

gas stationpetrol stationpumpfuelcanopywindshieldtanksnack

Say this to your child

“"Gas station! The car is hungry — glug, glug, glug, drink up, car! Squeaky windshield — squeak, squeak — all clean! Click! Full tank! Now the driver pays inside... and sometimes a snack jumps in the bag. It happens."”

Step by step

  1. The car rolls in under the big canopy — every gas station has one, tall enough for trucks.
  2. A grown-up opens the car’s little door on the side — that is where the tank drinks.
  3. The pump handle squeezes: glug, glug, glug — the numbers on the screen spin like a fast clock.
  4. Squeak, squeak — the windshield gets a wash while the tank fills.
  5. Click! The tank is full, the nozzle goes home, and the driver pays inside — where the snacks live, and where the driver usually buys exactly one.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, two fuel pumps stand under the canopy with a water-drop sign above — the pumps are the kitchen, the drop is the menu, and every car in town is a regular.

Ask your child

"Who touches the pump?" (a grown-up — always) "What sound does the windshield make?" (squeak, squeak) "What does the car drink?" (gas — or petrol in the UK)

What your child can say or do

Your child might count the pump screen’s spinning numbers out loud, command the windshield wash with spray-bottle authority at home, or appoint themselves snack commissioner for every fill-up, forever.

Out in the real world

American and Canadian families fill up with gas; British families fill up with petrol — the station answers to both names. Pumps are strictly grown-up territory in all three countries, and the card says so kindly: look, don’t touch, wait in the seat.

Try it together

Car wash and fill-up for ride-ons: chalk prices on paper, a "pump" that counts to ten while filling (one squeeze per number), windshield wiped with a real cloth. Ten is the magic number — every fill-up is a counting exercise.

Understanding check

Ask: "Who uses the pump?" (grown-ups) "What do we count while the tank fills?" (one to ten — glug, glug...)

This lesson pairs with the Gas Station flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Bus Stop — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the whole first bus ride — waiting, boarding, riding and ringing — before the real one happens.

What is this?

A bus stop is a little shelter with a bench and a sign, where the bus arrives on a schedule to carry everyone along its route.

What does it mean?

Shared rides are the idea: one big bus, one driver, and a whole street of people going the same way — the town’s moving meeting room.

What does the child need to know?

You need the timetable (when does the bus come?), a fare or a tap-card, and the patience of the bench — the bus runs on its own clock, not ours.

Why this matters

Not everyone has a car, and even cars stay home sometimes — the bus carries the whole town: to school, to work, to the pool, and home again.

What it teaches

Waiting for a schedule, boarding in turn, sitting while riding, and the stop-button decision — timing a press is real planning for small hands.

Words to learn

bus stopbusshelterbenchtimetabledriverfaretapstop buttonroute

Say this to your child

“"The bus stop! Bench, timetable, watch the street... HERE IT COMES! Wave! Tap — beep! Find a seat. The town rolls past the window — look, the bakery! Bing! Our stop! Step down — bus ride complete!"”

Step by step

  1. Check the timetable — the bus comes at its own time, and the timetable knows it.
  2. Wait on the bench and watch down the street — a big shape with lights is getting closer...
  3. Wave! Board in turn and tap the card — beep! — then find a seat or hold the pole like a sailor.
  4. Watch the windows: the town scrolls by — the bakery! the library! — count the stops.
  5. Press the stop button a little early — bing! — the driver nods, the bus slows, and off you step, right where you planned.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the shelter stands with a big round bus sign and a bench inside — the smallest building in town, and one of the busiest.

Ask your child

"What do we do while we wait?" (sit on the bench, watch for the bus) "What do we tap when we get on?" (our card — beep!) "When do we press the button?" (a little before our stop — bing!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might run a full bus route through the house with cushion stops, ring an invisible bell for the refrigerator stop, or wave at real buses with such commitment that drivers wave back (they always do).

Out in the real world

Waiting in line is a queue in the UK and a line in the US and Canada — both start at a bus stop. Practicing the bench-wave-tap-sit routine at home makes the first real ride smooth, and the stop button becomes a trusted friend.

Try it together

Bus route around the house: chairs in a line, tickets torn from paper, stops called at the fridge (Stop 1: Kitchen), the bookshelf (Stop 2: Library) and the bathroom (Stop 3: Splash Pools). Driver rotates every lap — bing!

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do at the shelter?" (wait for the bus) "What do we press before our stop?" (the button — bing!)

This lesson pairs with the Bus Stop flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Train Station — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches how a train ride begins — the board, the platform, the wind of the arriving train.

What is this?

A train station is where trains stop for passengers: platforms, a big clock, a departures board, and trains that arrive exactly when they say they will.

What does it mean?

Running on time is the idea: the whole station obeys the clock, and that is how hundreds of trains a day never bump into each other.

What does the child need to know?

You need your platform number (from the big board), your ticket, and one rule learned well: stand BEHIND the yellow line until the train stops.

Why this matters

Trains carry more people than cars ever could, faster and together — and the station is where the whole town lines up to go somewhere wonderful.

What it teaches

Reading a departures board (numbers!), platform following, the yellow-line safety habit, and schedule respect — trains wait for nobody, and children learn it kindly, once.

Words to learn

train stationrailway stationplatformtrackdepartures boardticketconductorall aboardyellow line

Say this to your child

“"The train station! The big board says: platform 2! We stand behind the yellow line... WHOOSH — here it comes! Doors beep open — all aboard! Clickety-clack, clickety-clack — off we go!"”

Step by step

  1. Read the big board: our train, our time, our PLATFORM — a number to remember (2 is a good one).
  2. Walk to platform 2 — follow the signs, the arrows know the way.
  3. Stand behind the yellow line — trains arrive with wind, and the line is the safe side of it.
  4. WHOOSH — the train slides in, the doors open with a polite beep, and everyone boards in turn.
  5. Find seats, watch the town run backwards out the window — clickety-clack — and listen for the conductor’s punch: your ticket’s journey begins.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the station clock rules the roof and the train nose pokes out of the arch — the clock is not decoration; the whole station obeys it, and the train waits for nobody.

Ask your child

"What do we look for on the big board?" (our platform number) "Where do we stand when the train comes?" (behind the yellow line) "What sound does the train make on the rails?" (clickety-clack)

What your child can say or do

Your child might punch paper tickets with a hole punch all afternoon, call "all aboard!" at the sofa with conductor gravity, or become the family’s official platform-number rememberer — a position for life.

Out in the real world

American families say train station; British families also say railway station — same platforms, same wind. Trains run to the minute in all three countries, which makes the station a child’s first honest lesson in what a schedule really is.

Try it together

Station at home: the sofa is platform 1, tickets punched with a hole punch, the conductor calls "all aboard!" and clips every ticket, and the train leaves exactly on time — the clock on the card is the boss.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do we stand before the train arrives?" (behind the yellow line) "Who is the boss of the station?" (the clock — trains run on the minute)

This lesson pairs with the Train Station flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Airport — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what an airport is and what happens there — from rolling suitcase to climbing airplane.

What is this?

An airport is where airplanes take off and land, and where travelers check in their suitcases, wait in big bright rooms, and climb aboard.

What does it mean?

Doors to everywhere is the idea: the airport is the town’s biggest door — it opens onto every other place on the map.

What does the child need to know?

You need a suitcase with your name on it, a boarding pass, and shoes that slip off easily — airports ask everyone the same kind steps.

Why this matters

Some family lives too far for a car — a day of driving becomes a few hours of flying, and the whole swap happens in a building with a tower watching the sky.

What it teaches

Sequencing a big trip, name-tag awareness (your suitcase is YOURS), the patience of airport waiting, and the physics show outside the window — planes really do bend up into the sky.

Words to learn

airportairplaneaeroplanesuitcaseboarding passtowertake offlandingwingstrip

Say this to your child

“"The airport! Suitcases roll — brrrrumble — the tower watches the sky, and THERE: the airplane takes off — vrrroooom, up, up and away! One day that will be us, waving at the whole town from the window!"”

Step by step

  1. Roll the suitcase in — wheels singing, name tag facing out.
  2. Check in: the suitcase rides a belt and disappears (do not worry — it meets you at the other end, that is the deal).
  3. Walk the big bright rooms, follow the signs, and look UP — the windows are airplane television.
  4. Watch the tower work: it talks to the planes, and the planes listen — take off means climbing right over your head.
  5. One day soon: your row is called, you walk the tunnel, buckle up, and the town becomes tiny below the window.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the pink airplane climbs right past the control tower — the tower is the airport’s eye, and every take-off happens under its watch.

Ask your child

"Who talks to the airplanes?" (the tower) "Where does the big suitcase go?" (on the belt — it meets us at the other end) "What does the airplane do at take-off?" (climbs — up, up and away)

What your child can say or do

Your child might line up kitchen chairs as an airplane and call rows by number, tag every stuffed animal with a paper name label, or stand at the real airport window calling every landing like an air-traffic announcer.

Out in the real world

It is an airplane to American families and an aeroplane to British families — and either way it leaves from the airport. Many airports have free viewing spots where jets land right over your head; the score-each-landing game is a classic for a reason.

Try it together

Front-row plane spotting: find the viewing spot, score each landing, guess the destination from the colors, and practice the wave — every pilot appreciates it, and one or two flash the lights back.

Understanding check

Ask: "Where do the suitcases go at check-in?" (on the belt — to meet us at the other end) "What watches every take-off?" (the tower)

This lesson pairs with the Airport flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Community Garden — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches how a shared garden works — and how to grow the first plant a child ever grows.

What is this?

A community garden is a shared patch where neighbors each grow something — carrots, beans, sunflowers — in plots and planter boxes side by side.

What does it mean?

Growing together is the idea: nobody could eat a whole row of beans, so a garden feeds the whole street, and everyone waters someone else’s carrots at least once.

What does the child need to know?

You need soil, seeds (radishes and beans are the friendly ones), water, and a secret ingredient that cannot be rushed: days.

Why this matters

Food comes from somewhere — and a child who pulls up a carrot they grew understands "somewhere" forever after, in a way no picture book can teach.

What it teaches

Sequencing (seed, sprout, plant, food), patience across weeks, responsibility on a watering schedule, and naming roots, stems, leaves and flowers on sight.

Words to learn

gardencommunityplotplanterseedsproutwaterweedrootsharvestgrow

Say this to your child

“"The community garden! Everyone on the street grows something here. Seeds in — tuck, pat, pat. Water — gentle rain, gentle rain. Weeds — out you go, not invited! And one day... a SPROUT! We grew that!"”

Step by step

  1. Look at the plots: every box belongs to a neighbor, and every box looks different — that is the fun of it.
  2. Plant the seeds in a shallow line, cover them like a blanket, and pat the soil — tuck them in, literally.
  3. Water on a schedule — gentle rain, not a flood; the watering can is a job, not a toy (okay, it is a little bit a toy).
  4. Weed kindly: some plants are not invited, and pulling them gives the carrots the room.
  5. Wait — one week, two weeks — and then the sprout. The sprout is a national holiday. Take a picture.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the wooden planter box holds a young sprout, carrots with green tops and leafy plants — a whole harvest in one box, and every bit of it was water somebody carried.

Ask your child

"Who grows things in a community garden?" (the neighbors — everyone together) "What do seeds need?" (soil, water, sunshine and days) "What do we do with weeds?" (pull them — kindly, but out)

What your child can say or do

Your child might measure their sprout with a paper ruler every single morning, name the sunflower, or defend the strawberry patch from the family dog with treaty-level diplomacy.

Out in the real world

The British keep private plots called allotments; American and Canadian towns share community gardens — same dirt, same pride. Children who grow a vegetable eat the vegetable: the oldest trick in the parenting book, and it works.

Try it together

Claim a window box as the family plot: plant radishes or beans (fast, forgiving, exciting to pull up), water on a schedule, and measure the sprout with a paper ruler every Sunday. The wait is the lesson.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do seeds need to grow?" (soil, water, sun — and days) "Who owns the community garden?" (nobody and everybody — the neighbors share it)

This lesson pairs with the Community Garden flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Park — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what parks are for — running, resting, tree meetings — and why the grass belongs to everyone.

What is this?

A park is a big green space that belongs to the whole town: grass for running, trees for shade, benches for resting, open from morning to evening.

What does it mean?

Shared green is the idea: no one owns the park, so everyone does — the town keeps it free on purpose, like a giant front lawn for everybody.

What does the child need to know?

You need running shoes, a ball or a kite or nothing at all, and a drink for the bench break. The tree provides the shade; you provide the visit.

Why this matters

Towns are full of hard, busy places — the park is the soft, slow one. Every person in town, every single day, is allowed to just... be in it.

What it teaches

Big-movement play (run, roll, climb), sensory noticing (bark, leaves, birdsong), sharing open space kindly, and the rarest preschool skill: doing nothing, happily, on a bench.

Words to learn

parkgrasstreeshadebenchlamppostpathpicnicfresh airseasons

Say this to your child

“"The park! Run the grass — fast, faster, flop! Meet the big tree — feel the bark, find the shade. Play the ball game, chase the pigeon politely... and rest on the bench. Ahh. The park is the town’s big green breath."”

Step by step

  1. Come in by the path — parks always have one, and it leads past everything.
  2. Run the grass: the soft field is the town’s biggest "yes" — run, roll, lie down, look at clouds.
  3. Meet the tree: bark by hand, leaves by shape, and the shade test — stand under it and feel the difference.
  4. Play your game — ball, kite, chase — and when the legs get heavy...
  5. The bench. The lamppost. The long slow breath. Parks end every visit the same way: sitting in the shade, being glad the town kept this.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, one enormous tree does the heavy lifting over the bench and the lamppost — parks are measured by their shade, and this one has plenty.

Ask your child

"Who does the park belong to?" (everyone in town — nobody and everybody) "What does the big tree give us on a hot day?" (shade) "What do we do when our legs get heavy?" (rest on the bench)

What your child can say or do

Your child might adopt one tree with a name and a birthday, lie on the grass naming cloud animals until further notice, or treat the bench as the official finish line of every park visit, forever.

Out in the real world

Every US, UK and Canadian town keeps at least one park free for everyone, and the bench is the universal invitation to slow down. The tree on the card is decades old — parks are gifts from townsfolk long gone, kept for the townsfolk still coming.

Try it together

Meet-a-tree day: pick one tree, learn its bark by hand and its leaves by shape, and visit it every season — spring buds, summer shade, autumn colors, winter branches. One tree makes the whole park personal.

Understanding check

Ask: "What does the park cost?" (nothing — it is free for everyone) "What do we do under the big tree?" (rest in the shade — the long slow breath)

This lesson pairs with the Park flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Playground — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches the playground — how each piece works and the two big rules that make it fun for everyone.

What is this?

A playground is a place built for playing: a slide, swings, a climbing frame, usually on soft ground, usually full of other kids doing exactly the same thing.

What does it mean?

Turn-taking is the idea: the best slide in town is best because everyone gets a turn — the playground is sharing, made out of metal and sunshine.

What does the child need to know?
