You need grippy shoes, turn-taking patience, and the two big rules loaded: one at a time on the slide, and never grab a moving swing.

Why this matters

Wiggles have to go somewhere — the playground is where they go to be used up, loudly, with other children, in the fresh air.

What it teaches

Climbing strength, turn-taking, swing pumping (lean and stretch — the rhythm finds itself), and the brave first slide of every new season, when the slide looks taller than last year.

Words to learn

playgroundslideswingladderclimbturnwaitpumproundaboutmerry-go-round

Say this to your child

“"The playground! Up the ladder — step, step — check the bottom is clear... WHEEE, down the slide! Off, away, back of the line. Now the swings — lean back, pump, pump — higher! The playground is where the wiggles live!"”

Step by step

  1. Up the ladder — step, step, step, hands hold the rails.
  2. Top of the slide: sit, check that nobody is at the bottom, then... WHEEE! Feet first, always.
  3. Off, away, and to the back of the line — one at a time is the rule, and the line moves fast when everyone follows it.
  4. The swings: sit, lean back, pump the legs — stretch, fold, stretch, fold — higher, higher!
  5. The circuit: one turn on everything, then a favorite — and when the swing must stop, let it stop. Never grab a moving swing; waiting is a playground superpower.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, all three classics ride together — the slide, the swing frame and the climbing ladder — the trio every playground in the world is built around.

Ask your child

"What do we check before we slide?" (nobody at the bottom) "How do we go higher on the swing?" (lean back and pump the legs) "What are the two big rules?" (one at a time on the slide — never grab a moving swing)

What your child can say or do

Your child might run the circuit with referee-level rule enforcement, discover swing-pumping on a random Tuesday and demand witnesses, or name the slide like a roller coaster with a grand opening every spring.

Out in the real world

British playgrounds often add a roundabout (the US says merry-go-round), and the see-saw answers to teeter-totter across the border — every town names the same joy differently. Swings are the starter: pumping by yourself is a real independence day.

Try it together

Playground circuit: one trip on each thing, then choose a favorite and do it three more times. Teach the two big rules kindly — one at a time on the slide, and wait for the swing to stop before you grab it.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we do at the top of the slide?" (sit, check, then feet first) "What do we do when we want the swing?" (wait for it to stop — never grab it)

This lesson pairs with the Playground flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Recycling Center — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches where recycling goes and why sorting matters — the journey from bin to something brand new.

What is this?

A recycling center is where the town’s bottles, cans, paper and cardboard arrive to be sorted and sent off to become things again.

What does it mean?

Second chances is the idea: most "trash" is not trash yet — sorted right, it comes back as new bottles, new paper, new boxes.

What does the child need to know?

You need to know the teams: paper, plastic, glass, cans — and the golden rule, rinsed and empty, every time.

Why this matters

The planet only has so much new stuff in it — recycling keeps the old stuff in the game, and the center is where the town hands it back in.

What it teaches

Sorting by material (a real classification skill), the rinse-and-empty habit, understanding loops and arrows, and the pride of being the household’s strictest inspector.

Words to learn

recyclingrecyclebinsortpaperplasticglasscanscardboardarrowssecond life

Say this to your child

“"The recycling center! Rinse it — swish! Sort it — paper HERE, plastic THERE, stomp the cardboard — CRUNCH! Into the bins, off to the factory... and one day it comes BACK as something new! Round and round, the arrows never stop!"”

Step by step

  1. Meet the sign: three arrows chasing each other in a loop — round and round, never stopping. That is recycling, drawn as a picture.
  2. Empty and rinse first — a jar with jam in it is still jam; a rinsed jar is glass, ready for its second life.
  3. Sort: paper HERE, plastic THERE, cardboard in the middle — stomp it flat first, the crunch is mandatory.
  4. Bring it to the center: each material rides its own bin, like teams boarding different buses.
  5. Off it goes to the factory — and weeks later, somewhere in town, a new bottle or box says hello. The loop closes. The arrows were right.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, three chasing arrows spin in the arch over the doors — reduce, reuse, recycle, in the order the planet prefers, drawn as a loop that never ends.

Ask your child

"What do the three arrows mean?" (things come back as new things — the loop) "What do we do before we recycle a jar?" (empty it and rinse it) "Which bin does cardboard go in?" (its own team — after a good stomp)

What your child can say or do

Your child might appoint themselves Sorting Inspector with a clipboard, stomp every box with professional enthusiasm, or correct a visiting relative’s bin technique with the confidence of a health-and-safety officer.

Out in the real world

American families carry garbage or trash to the curb; British families carry the rubbish — and the recycling bin is the green one almost everywhere. Kids are famously the strictest sorters in the house; hand them the job and the title.

Try it together

Home sorting line: three boxes for paper, plastic and cans, and a "quality inspector" who checks each item and stamps it through. The inspector role rotates — and the sorting habit sticks for life.

Understanding check

Ask: "What happens to things we recycle?" (they become something new — second life) "What is the first step?" (empty and rinse — then sort)

This lesson pairs with the Recycling Center flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Sports Center — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches what a sports center is and how to try a new game there — rain or shine.

What is this?

A sports center is a big building full of ways to move: a swimming pool, courts for ball games, a gym, and a timetable of classes for every age.

What does it mean?

A roof over play is the idea: rain cannot cancel games that live indoors — the sports center keeps the town moving all winter.

What does the child need to know?

You need sport shoes, a water bottle, and the one thing nobody can lend you: the willingness to try something new in front of strangers who are all trying too.

Why this matters

Not every family has a garden big enough for games — the center shares one with the whole town, plus a pool that steams in January.

What it teaches

Trying new movements (splash, bounce, balance), following a class leader, water confidence, and the social skill of joining a game already in progress.

Words to learn

sports centerleisure centrepoolcourtgymclasstimetableteamtryshoes

Say this to your child

“"The sports center! Look at the board — swimming today! Shoes on, bottle filled, towel over the shoulder. Into the shallow end — splash! Kick those legs! And when class is done we say the magic words: AGAIN tomorrow!"”

Step by step

  1. Read the timetable together — the wall board lists everything: swim times, ball times, tiny-gym times.
  2. Pack the kit: shoes, bottle, towel, and the lucky sock if there is one (there is always one).
  3. Try the thing: the pool (splash in the shallow end first — everyone does), the court, the soft floor.
  4. Copy the leader — arms up, arms down — nobody is watching anyone else; they are all busy wobbling too.
  5. Finish with water and the two words: "AGAIN tomorrow." The timetable says yes.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the round window rolls in like a soccer ball over the sports center doors — the building plays too, and it is telling you so.

Ask your child

"What lives at the sports center?" (a pool, courts, classes — every game under one roof) "What do we bring?" (shoes, a water bottle, a towel) "What are the magic words at the end?" (AGAIN tomorrow!)

What your child can say or do

Your child might run family mini-olympics with paper medals and a mandatory anthem, copy the class leader so faithfully the leader notices, or post the timetable results on the fridge like league tables.

Out in the real world

American families say sports center; British families say leisure centre — same courts, same chlorine smell. Most centers run cheap kids’ swim and soft-play sessions; the timetable is a whole winter’s worth of Tuesdays.

Try it together

Family mini-olympics on any flat floor: sock-ball toss into laundry baskets, hallway bowling, a balance-beam line of tape, medal ceremony at the end — paper medals, national anthem optional, absolutely sung.

Understanding check

Ask: "Why do games keep going when it rains?" (they live indoors — under the roof) "What do we say after class?" (AGAIN tomorrow!)

This lesson pairs with the Sports Center flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Places in the Community.

PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY LESSON · PLACES IN THE COMMUNITY · AGES 3–5 YEARS

Zoo — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches how to visit the zoo like a real explorer — a plan, a quest, and kind quiet voices.

What is this?

A zoo is a big park where animals from all over the world live, and visitors walk from habitat to habitat to meet them: lions, penguins, giraffes and more.

What does it mean?

Meeting the world is the idea: the zoo is the only afternoon walk that passes through five continents.

What does the child need to know?

You need comfortable shoes, a map (or a plan of three animals), quiet voices, and walking feet — animals spook at shouting and running.

Why this matters

Most animals live where we cannot go — deserts, ice, treetops — the zoo brings them close enough to watch, learn about, and care about for the rest of your life.

What it teaches

Animal naming and grouping (big, small, striped, spotted), reading name plates (where it lives, what it eats), quiet-voice practice, and empathy for creatures with very different days than ours.

Words to learn

zooanimalhabitatlionpenguingiraffeelephantname platequestzookeeper

Say this to your child

“"The zoo! Here is the map — today we find THREE animals: the lion, the penguin, and the funny-named one! Quiet feet... look — the lion is stretching! The plate says: Africa, meat-eater, sleeps 20 hours. Wow. Penguins next!"”

Step by step

  1. Come in the gate and grab the map — every good expedition starts with a map.
  2. Pick the quest: three animals — one big, one small, one with a funny name. Write them down or remember them hard.
  3. Walk to animal one. Watch for a full minute — animals are busy; give them a moment to do something amazing.
  4. Read the name plate together: where does it live? what does it eat? Every plate is a tiny passport.
  5. Quiet voices all day, especially at the penguins — they are doing their important fish business. Three animals, deeply seen, beats thirty rushed ones.

Look closer at the picture

On the card, the gates stand open under the big ZOO sign with round bushes standing guard — the doors to the one walk in town that crosses five continents.

Ask your child

"What do the name plates tell us?" (the animal’s name, where it lives, what it eats) "What kind of voices at the zoo?" (quiet ones) "How many animals on the quest?" (three — one big, one small, one funny-named)

What your child can say or do

Your child might adopt the penguin enclosure as a second home, narrate the lion like a nature documentary, or remember the okapi’s funny name for a full year and deploy it at dinner parties.

Out in the real world

The zoo is the same word on both shores, but the penguin feeding is the universal favorite in the US, UK and Canada. The gates on the card open onto the first geography lesson a child ever takes — every animal brings its own map.

Try it together

Pick three animals before you go — one big, one small, one with a funny name — and make them the quest. Read each plate out loud: three real facts beat a rushed lap of everything.

Understanding check

Ask: "What do we read at every enclosure?" (the name plate — where it lives, what it eats) "How do we walk at the zoo?" (quiet feet, walking, no running)
